description: We’re a team passionate about learning, with backgrounds in engineering, psychology, ergonomics and languages. By combining how people think, communicate and design, we build smart, practical solutions that make technology truly useful and accessible. Why join us? We work in a region that isn’t always at the forefront of tech, but we refuse to be left behind. We see those challenges as a reason to be more creative, stay sharp and keep pushing forward.
summary: “IAlejandro Aprende” is an illustrated children’s story about the equipment NASA left on the Moon. Its first adventure, “Lunar Ride with No Brakes,” follows Manuel, Caro, Jaky, and NASAsha, Alejandro’s real-life pet, a little dog in an astronaut suit, as they leave the “NASA parking lot” in a lunar vehicle while IAlejandro waits at home, watching the sky. Along the way they find four real Apollo and Surveyor objects: the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), the laser retroreflector, the seismometer, and the Surveyor 3 probe. After each scene, an information box explains when it was sent, what it was for, a fun fact, and its environmental impact. Finally, IAlejandro and NASAsha disinfect the car and check their health before traveling to avoid carrying microorganisms to the Moon, and the story closes with a lesson: “Even on the Moon we leave our mark, but not always in the best way.” With humor and relatable characters, the project turns the history of discarded equipment into a fun read that sparks children’s curiosity about space and invites them to value what we leave behind. It comes in digital and print, in Spanish and English, and each object includes an interactive 3D image.

Prezi in English: Unstoppable Moonwalk

WHAT DOES IT DO OR HOW DOES IT WORK?
“IAlejandro Aprende” works as a digital story divided into eight chapters, where real objects left on the Moon by NASA are presented through a comical situation: children bounce around due to low gravity in the lunar rover, a mirror reflects a laser back at them, a “moonquake” turns out to be NASAsha’s rumbling hungry belly, and a probe missing its camera seems “stolen,” even though astronauts actually took it back to study it. After each scene, an info box appears featuring a NASA photograph, four fixed questions (When was it sent?, What for?, What did it do?, and Did you know…?), and a closing note on its environmental impact, allowing the reader to separate the adventure from the verified facts. NASAsha is not an invented character: she is Alejandro’s real-life pet, which makes the story more relatable to children. In the end, IAlejandro decides to travel with NASAsha to see the objects with his own eyes; before taking off, both disinfect their car and check their health (planetary protection), and upon arriving at the Moon, they discover more objects. The story ends with a box featuring NASAsha’s lesson on caring for the worlds we explore and a five-question mini-challenge. The “discarded” space equipment can also be explored as interactive 3D images. The story is available in both digital and printed formats, in Spanish and English, so it can be read on a screen or on paper.


WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT OFFER?
The project turns technical information into simple and memorable learning. It fosters reading and scientific curiosity, teaches concepts such as lunar gravity, the absence of sound in a vacuum, and measuring distances with light, and shows that the equipment left in space continues to provide knowledge: the retroreflector is still used to measure the distance to the Moon, and the recovered parts of Surveyor 3 helped us understand how materials age outside of Earth. It also raises environmental awareness: humanity has left nearly 200 tons of waste on the Moon, and the story explains planetary protection and the responsibility not to pollute the worlds we explore. Furthermore, it uses data from official NASA sources, providing confidence to families and teachers. Being available in digital and printed versions makes it accessible to those without a computer or internet connection, and its English version allows readers to practice the language and reach a wider audience.


WHAT IS THE EXPECTED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT?
An educational, social, and environmental impact is expected: bringing the history of lunar exploration closer to primary school children and their families using relatable characters, in both digital and printed versions and in two languages (Spanish and English) to reach those without computers, and sparking an interest in science from an early age. It also seeks to raise responsible explorers who understand that caring for the environment doesn't stop on Earth, to have teachers use it as a reading resource in the classroom, and for the “IAlejandro Aprende” series to grow with new adventures about the equipment NASA has left on Mars and in deep space, promoting a simple idea: what is left in space also tells a story.


WHAT TOOLS, PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE WERE USED TO DEVELOP THE PROJECT?
We used Google Drive and Google Docs for collaborative writing, supported by Word for final formatting; Canva to fully design the pages, the cover, and the illustrations of the story; the physical "Nacho" primer as a complementary pedagogical resource to strengthen basic learning; and the Claude and Gemini AIs to create the interactive 3D images of the "discarded" space equipment and organize the project's deployment on Netlify. The data for the story was taken from official sources like NASA, the USGS, and the International Laser Ranging Service (ILRS), supplemented by scientific and journalistic sources regarding the environmental impact on the Moon, and the photographs in the infoboxes are NASA images. The website and the 3D images were built as web pages (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using the Three.js library for 3D), generated with the help of AI and published on Netlify. No specialized hardware was required.


HOW CREATIVE IS YOUR PROJECT?
The project is creative because it presents "discarded" space equipment as if they were characters with a story, rather than just space junk. It uses humor (the "moonquake" that is actually NASAsha's belly), a real-life pet (NASAsha, Alejandro's dog), and a narrator who doesn't travel at first (IAlejandro), which prompts the final question: what if instead of being told about it, we go see it for ourselves? The scene-plus-infobox structure allows the child to have fun first and learn later, and each box closes by showing the environmental impact of the object, so the story combines narrative, science, verified data, and environmental care in a single format, which is also delivered in both digital and print.


WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?
We considered the readers' age, which is why we used simple language, short scenes, and a fun tone with relatable characters. We also prioritized scientific accuracy: every piece of data in the info boxes (year, mission, purpose, fun fact, and environmental impact) was taken from official sources like NASA and the USGS, and verified against them. Another factor was the structure: each scene is followed by a box with the same four questions and a final note on environmental impact, so readers can distinguish the adventure from the verified data. We also wanted to show the other side of exploration: the debris left on the Moon and the importance of planetary protection; that's why the characters disinfect their rover before traveling, and the story ends with a lesson on caring for the worlds we explore. Finally, we chose objects from the Apollo and Surveyor missions that are real, well-documented, and easy to relate to everyday ideas like jumping, mirrors, earthquakes, and cameras.
